title: "Verifying output"
subtitle: "The most important habit on this site."
---

::: {.callout-warning}
**This is the page that matters most.** Every other shortcut is fine if
you do this one thing. Skip this and you will eventually publish something
wrong with your name on it.
:::

## The rule

Read the diff. Run the code. Open the file. Compare to your expectation.

Every time, even when you're tired.

## Outline — what "verify" means in concrete cases

### Code edits

- Read the diff before accepting. Quarto, Stata, R, Python, LaTeX —
  doesn't matter. If you're not reading diffs, you're not in control.
- For multi-file changes, read every file's diff. The boring ones are
  where the bugs hide.

### Numerical output

- If Claude reports a coefficient, **re-run the regression yourself** in
  your usual environment before believing it. Cloud LLMs can confidently
  report numbers from a hallucinated run.
- For estimation, save random seeds explicitly and confirm reproducibility
  on a re-run.

### Citations and references

- Any new `\cite{...}` Claude adds: **confirm the entry exists** in your
  `.bib` and that the cited paper actually says what you're attributing
  to it. See [Hallucinations](../pitfalls/hallucinations.qmd).

### Files that disappear

- For deletions, refactors, or replication-package reorganization, work
  in a copy, not in your live project. Or use git: commit before, branch,
  and you can always undo.

## Outline — habits that make verification cheap

- Use git. Even if you don't push to GitHub, commit locally before any
  big change so `git diff` is meaningful.
- Use plan mode for multi-file changes. Reading a plan first and then
  reviewing the diffs that match it is much easier than parsing surprise
  edits.
- Run the build/test after every change. If your project has a `make`
  or a master `do` file, ask Claude to run it after each meaningful edit.

> Tell me which of these you'd most like fully worked through.
